bodyHtml:
Volume profile tells you where trade happened. Order flow tells you how it happened: who crossed the spread, who waited, and what was sitting in the book when they did. Before any footprint chart or delta reading makes sense, you need a clear picture of the plumbing: the kinds of orders, the order book, and how an exchange actually matches a buyer with a seller.

This chapter is about CME Group futures (ES, NQ, GC, CL), because that is where the order flow is visible. Every trade on CME Globex goes through one central order book with public data, which is what makes the tools in the rest of the track possible. VP-10 explains why spot forex is different.

Market orders and limit orders

A limit order says "buy (or sell) at this price or better". The SEC's investor guide puts it plainly: a buy limit executes only at the limit price or lower, a sell limit only at the limit price or higher. If nobody is willing to trade at that price yet, the order rests in the book and waits. Limit orders provide liquidity: they are the prices other traders can hit.

A market order says "buy (or sell) now at the best available price". It executes immediately against whatever limit orders are resting, but the price is not guaranteed. Market orders take liquidity. In order-flow language, the market order is the aggressor and the limit order is the passive side. CME's own order-type guide adds a detail worth knowing: on Globex a "market" order is typically handled as a market-limit order, which executes at the best available price and, if only partly filled, turns the rest into a limit order at that price. Stop orders sit outside the book until price reaches the stop level, then enter as market or limit orders. That is why a cluster of stops, once triggered, arrives as a burst of aggressive orders.

This is the link to liquidity in the core course (chapter 07). When traders say stops sit above equal highs, they mean a pile of buy stops that will become market buys the moment price trades there.

The order book and the DOM

The order book is the list of all resting limit orders at every price. Most platforms display it as a vertical ladder called the DOM (depth of market). Bids are on one side, asks on the other, prices in the middle. The highest bid is the best bid, the lowest ask is the best ask, and the gap between them is the spread. In ES the minimum price step, or tick, is 0.25 index points, and the spread is usually one tick.

Two types of book data exist on CME. Market by price (MBP) shows the total quantity at each price level. Market by order (MBO) shows each individual order, with its size and queue position, identified only by an anonymous order ID. CME's MBO FAQ notes it carries no customer-identifying information. Tools that claim to spot icebergs or individual large orders rely on MBO data (see VP-09).

How a trade matches: price, then time

A trade happens when an aggressive order meets a resting one. CME describes this as matching resting orders with aggressing orders using its matching algorithms. For ES and most equity index futures the algorithm is FIFO (first in, first out): the best price is filled first, and at the same price, the order that arrived earliest is filled first. CME's documentation says FIFO uses price and time as its only criteria.

This queue priority is why some traders care about where they sit in line. CME's rules also say that an order loses its place, and goes to the back of the queue, if its quantity is increased or its price is changed. Not every CME product uses pure FIFO: the exchange also runs pro-rata and other allocation methods for some contracts, so check the product if you trade outside index futures.

Worked example: a market buy sweeps the book

Take the book shown above. A trader sends a 75-lot market buy. There are only 22 contracts offered at the best ask, so the order fills through several prices in turn:

PriceContracts filledNote
5,200.5022level emptied
5,200.7538level emptied
5,201.001526 left resting

The buyer's average price is 5,200.727, a little worse than the 5,200.50 best ask they saw, because the order was larger than the quantity available at one price. That difference is slippage. It also moved the market: the last trade printed at 5,201.00, and until new sellers step in, the best ask has moved up.

This is the most important idea in order flow. Price moves when aggressive orders consume the resting liquidity at a price. A thin book moves easily; a thick one absorbs a lot of aggression without moving. Every footprint pattern in the next two chapters is some version of this.

Worked example: waiting in the queue

Now look at it from the passive side. Suppose you place a 3-lot sell limit at 5,200.50 just after trader D. Under FIFO you are fifth in line, with 43 contracts ahead of you. The 22-lot buy from the FIFO example fills 22 of them, which leaves 21 still ahead. For your order to fill completely, another 24 contracts of buying must trade at 5,200.50, assuming nobody ahead of you cancels. If they do cancel, you move up.

This is why passive traders care about queue position, and why a limit order is never a guaranteed fill. Price can trade at your level, print on the tape, and move away without ever reaching you. If you then change the price or add size, the CME rules above send you to the back of the queue again. When you backtest on charts, a "touch" of your limit price is not the same as a fill. Many traders count a fill only when price trades through the level by at least one tick.

Bid, ask and last on your chart

Candlestick charts are normally built from the last traded price. That hides the spread. When your platform shows a candle high at 5,201.00, it means a trade printed there; the best bid at that moment was one tick lower. For a long entry you pay the ask, and for a stop-loss on a long you usually sell at the bid. Over many trades those ticks add up, which is one reason order-flow traders think in ticks and dollars per tick rather than in candle prices.

Time and sales

Time and sales (the "tape") is the list of every trade: time, price, size, and whether it traded at the bid or the ask. A trade at the ask means a buyer was the aggressor; a trade at the bid means a seller was. Here is the same 75-lot sweep on the tape, followed by a few more trades:

TimePriceSizeTraded at
10:31:02.1145,200.5022ask
10:31:02.1145,200.7538ask
10:31:02.1145,201.0015ask
10:31:03.5205,200.254bid
10:31:04.0075,200.2512bid
10:31:05.8905,200.503ask

Notice that one order shows up as three prints at the same timestamp. Tape readers look for exactly that kind of burst. They also watch for the opposite: a stream of prints at the same price that doesn't move it, which is the start of the absorption idea in VP-09.

What a tick is worth

Order flow is read in ticks, so it helps to know what one tick is worth in money. These come from CME's contract specifications and Micro E-mini FAQ:

ContractTick sizeTick value
E-mini S&P 500 (ES)0.25 index pt$12.50
Micro E-mini S&P (MES)0.25 index pt$1.25
E-mini Nasdaq-100 (NQ)0.25 index pt$5.00
Micro E-mini Nasdaq (MNQ)0.25 index pt$0.50
Gold (GC)$0.10 per oz$10.00
Crude oil (CL)$0.01 per bbl$10.00

Spoofing: what the book cannot tell you

Resting orders can be cancelled at any time, so the book shows intentions, not commitments. Placing orders you intend to cancel before they execute is illegal: the U.S. Commodity Exchange Act, section 4c(a)(5)(C), prohibits "spoofing", described by the CFTC as bidding or offering with the intent to cancel before execution. It still happens, and it is one reason experienced order-flow traders put more weight on executed trades (the tape, the footprint) than on displayed size in the DOM.

Common mistakes

  • Treating large resting size as a wall. Displayed orders can be pulled in a millisecond.
  • Using market orders in thin conditions. Slippage can be several ticks around news or the open.
  • Assuming every exchange matches FIFO. Check the matching algorithm for the product.
  • Confusing "at the ask" with "buyers in control". It only says who crossed the spread on that trade.
  • Reading order flow on instruments without a central book. See VP-10.

Key takeaways

  • Limit orders rest and provide liquidity; market orders cross the spread and take it.
  • The DOM shows resting orders by price; MBO data shows individual orders anonymously.
  • CME index futures match FIFO: best price first, then earliest order.
  • Price moves when aggression consumes the resting liquidity at a price.
  • Time and sales records executed trades, which are more reliable than displayed size.

Practice exercises

  1. Rework the sweep with a 110-lot market buy. List each fill and the average price.
  2. Under FIFO, how would the queue example change if trader B had increased their order to 9 contracts before the buy arrived?
  3. Watch the ES DOM in a simulator for ten minutes around the cash open. Note how often the best bid or ask size changes without a trade.
  4. On the tape, find three bursts of prints with the same timestamp and note how many price levels each one crossed.

Self-check quiz

1. Which order provides liquidity: market or limit?

A limit order, because it rests in the book for others to trade against.

2. Two sell orders rest at the same price. Under FIFO, which fills first?

The one that arrived first.

3. Why did the 75-lot buy average above the best ask it saw?

Because the best ask only had 22 contracts; the rest filled at higher prices.

4. A trade prints at the bid. Who was the aggressor?

A seller, using a market (or marketable) order.

5. What does ES move per tick, in dollars, for one contract?

$12.50 (0.25 index points x $50).

6. Why do order-flow traders trust executed trades more than displayed size?

Displayed orders can be cancelled, and spoofing, though illegal, happens.

Sources

  2. Matching Algorithm Overview - CME Group
  3. Futures order types - CME Group education
  4. Investor Bulletin: Understanding Order Types - Investor.gov (SEC)
  5. Market by Order (MBO) FAQ - CME Group
  6. Micro E-mini Equity Index Futures FAQ (multipliers and ticks) - CME Group
  7. Gold Futures contract specs - CME Group
  8. Light Sweet Crude Oil Futures contract specs - CME Group
  9. Disruptive Trading Practices fact sheet (spoofing, CEA 4c(a)(5)(C)) - CFTC
